replacement: The voice stopped. It was a lackey’s tenor and a lackey’s song. Then a woman’s voice asked, in a coaxing and bashful tone, though with a mincing affectation:

“I could have gone further than this. I could have known more, if my fate hadn’t been against me from childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel for calling me names because I come from a filthy beggar and have no father. In Moscow they used to throw that in my teeth. The story had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch accuses me of rebelling against my birth, but I would have agreed to their killing me before I was born, so that I would never have come into the world at all. In the market they used to say it, and your mamma too, with a great lack of delicacy, began telling me that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say a wee bit when she might have said ‘a little bit,’ like everybody else? She wanted to make it touching, a proper peasant feeling. Can a Russian peasant be said to feel anything, next to an educated man? In his ignorance he can’t be said to have any feeling at all. Since I was a child, whenever I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I nearly burst with rage. I hate all Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”

“There’s no need for defense. In 1812 Napoleon, first Emperor of the French and father of the present one, made a great invasion of Russia. It would have been a good thing if they had conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and swallowed it up. We would have ended up with quite different institutions.”

“Yet he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. There he’s mistaken. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I’d have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey in how he behaves, how he thinks and how poor he is. He can’t do anything, and still everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with a bit of luck I could open a café restaurant in Petrovka, in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and in Moscow nobody’s cooking is special except the foreigners’. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, he’d fight him. And yet how is he better than I am? He’s ever so much stupider than I am. Look at all the money he’s thrown away for no reason!”

“On the contrary, it’s a coincidence that startles me,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Believe it or not, ever since that scene with her I’ve been thinking of nothing but my youthful greenness, and then you start in on exactly that, as if you’d guessed. Do you know what I’ve been telling myself, sitting here? Say I didn’t believe in life. Say I’d lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and was convinced that it’s all a disorderly, damnable, maybe devil-ridden chaos. Say I’d been hit by every horror of human disillusionment. I would still want to live. Once I’d tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away until I’d drained it! At thirty, though, I’m sure to put the cup down, even if I haven’t emptied it, and turn away—to where, I don’t know. But until thirty I know my youth will win out over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. Many times I’ve asked myself whether any despair exists that could beat this frantic and perhaps unseemly thirst for life in me. I’ve decided that none does—until I’m thirty, that is; after that it will leave me by itself, I imagine. Some driveling, consumptive moralists, poets especially, often call that thirst for life low. It is a Karamazov trait, true enough, this thirst for life whatever happens. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it low? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I long for life, and I keep on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves when they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though I lost faith in them long ago, perhaps; but from old habit the heart still treasures them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll leave from here. And yet I know I’m going only to a graveyard—but what a precious graveyard! The dead who lie there are precious. Every stone over them tells of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I’ll fall to the ground, kiss those stones and weep over them. Though I’m convinced in my heart that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep out of despair. I’ll weep simply because my tears will make me happy; I’ll soak my soul in the feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all there is to it. It has nothing to do with intellect or logic. It’s loving with your insides, with your stomach. You love the first strength of your youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.
